title: Notice of Adoption of Final Rule: Automated Employment Decision Tools
author: New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection

dom.t: Hiring audits: Disclosure cannot guarantee nondiscrimination

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source reports race- and intersection-specific applicant selection rates and impact ratios for automated employment decision tools. It does not address legal AI’s jagged task capabilities, selective deployment, human verification, or legal-work redesign, so its position relative to the cluster proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Employment screening: Audits reveal bias without remedying it
st.an: The final rule substantiates the cluster’s framing of Local Law 144 as a procedural audit, disclosure and notice regime rather than proof that bias is eliminated. It conditions AEDT use on a recent audit and transparency measures while expressly declining to guarantee an alternative selection process; it does not offer empirical evidence that audits produce fair outcomes.
qs: Local Law 144 of 2021 prohibits employers and employment agencies from using an automated employment decision tool unless the tool has been subject to a bias audit within one year of the use of the tool, information about the bias audit is publicly available, and certain notices have been provided to employees or job candidates.
Nothing in this subchapter requires an employer or employment agency to provide an           alternative selection process.

st.t: Hiring audits: Disclosure cannot guarantee nondiscrimination
st.an: The final rule directly supports the cluster’s account of a procedural compliance regime: it defines when audits are required, prescribes demographic calculations and disclosures, and mandates advance notice. It also expressly confirms that these transparency duties do not create a right to an alternative selection process. As a rulemaking document, it supplies no empirical evidence that audits guarantee or improve nondiscrimination outcomes.
qs: These rules generally clarify obligations of employers and employment agencies under the new law.
Nothing in this subchapter requires an employer or employment agency to provide an           alternative selection process.

mo.t: Automated decisions: Notice and recourse remain distinct rights
Solicitor entry: Diverse routes yield unequal attainment

kp.k: Employment AI use requires audits, publication, and notice
kp.d: DCWP's final rules implement Local Law 144 of 2021, which conditions employers' and employment agencies' use of automated employment decision tools (AEDTs) on a bias audit within one year, public audit information, and notices to employees or candidates. These are employment-domain regulatory requirements, not findings about AI's effects on legal services.
qs: Local Law 144 of 2021 prohibits employers and employment agencies from using an automated employment decision tool unless the tool has been subject to a bias audit within one year of the use of the tool, information about the bias audit is publicly available, and certain notices have been provided to employees or job candidates.
An employer or employment agency may not use or continue to use an AEDT if more than one year has passed since the most recent bias audit of the AEDT.

kp.k: Coverage turns on automated outputs' decision-making influence
kp.d: The rules specify three ways an output substantially assists or replaces discretionary decision-making: sole reliance, greater weight than any other individual criterion, or overriding conclusions from other factors, including human judgment. Coverage therefore does not depend solely on whether a human participates or makes the final hiring decision; the rule's example expressly includes early-stage screening.
qs: to use a simplified output to overrule conclusions derived from other factors including human decision-making.
This bias audit is necessary even though the employer is not using the AEDT to make the final hiring decision, but only to screen at an early point in the application process.

kp.k: Technical definitions distinguish predictions from transcription and translation
kp.d: The defined techniques generate predictions or classifications and involve a computer identifying, at least partly, inputs, their relative importance, and applicable model parameters to improve accuracy. Simplified outputs include scores, tags, categorizations, recommendations, and rankings, but exclude outputs that merely translate or transcribe existing text.
qs: for which a computer at least in part identifies the inputs, the relative importance placed on those inputs, and, if applicable, other parameters for the models in order to improve the accuracy of the prediction or classification.
It does not refer to the output from analytical tools that translate or transcribe existing text, e.g., convert a resume from a PDF or transcribe a video or audio interview.

kp.k: Auditors must satisfy independence and conflict restrictions
kp.d: An independent auditor must be capable of objective, impartial judgment. Prior or current involvement in using, developing, or distributing the AEDT disqualifies an auditor; employment relationships during the audit with a prospective or continuing user or relevant vendor also disqualify, as do direct or material indirect financial interests during the audit.
qs: “Independent auditor” means a person or group that is capable of exercising objective and impartial judgment on all issues within the scope of a bias audit of an AEDT.
is or was involved in using, developing, or distributing the AEDT;

kp.k: Selection audits require separate and intersectional demographic comparisons
kp.d: For tools selecting candidates or promotion employees to advance, or classifying them into groups, audits must calculate selection rates and impact ratios across EEO-1 categories. Comparisons must separately address sex, race/ethnicity, and their intersections; classification tools require calculations for each specified group. The statement of purpose describes these calculations as consistent with 29 C.F.R. § 1607.4. The supplied numerical tables are illustrative audit examples rather than empirical findings.
qs: Calculate the selection rate for each category;
Calculate the impact ratio for each category;
intersectional categories of sex, ethnicity, and race (e.g., impact ratio for selection of Hispanic or Latino male candidates vs. Not Hispanic or Latino Black or African American female candidates).
These calculations are consistent with Section 1607.4 of the EEOC Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures.

kp.k: Scoring audits compare above-median rates across demographic categories
kp.d: When AEDTs score applicants or employees considered for promotion, audits must calculate the full sample's median score, each category's scoring rate, and impact ratios, separately covering sex, race/ethnicity, and intersectional categories. A scoring rate measures the share above the sample median, rather than a category's average score; its impact ratio uses the highest category scoring rate as denominator.
qs: “Scoring Rate” means the rate at which individuals in a category receive a score above the sample’s median score, where the score has been calculated by an AEDT.
Calculate the median score for the full sample of applicants;

“Impact ratio” means either (1) the selection rate for a category divided by the selection rate of the most selected category or (2) the scoring rate for a category divided by the scoring rate for the highest scoring category.

kp.k: Unknown and small categories require transparent treatment
kp.d: Both selection and scoring audits must report how many assessed individuals were excluded from calculations because their category was unknown. Auditors may omit categories representing less than 2% of audit data from impact-ratio calculations, but must publish a justification, applicant counts, and the omitted category's selection or scoring rate.
qs: Indicate the number of individuals the AEDT assessed that are not included in the required calculations because they fall within an unknown category.

Where such a category is excluded, the summary of results must include the independent auditor’s justification for the exclusion, as well as the number of applicants and scoring rate or selection rate for the excluded category.

kp.k: Shared historical audits require users' own data contributions
kp.d: Historical data from AEDT use is the default audit basis and may be pooled across employers or agencies. An employer or agency may rely on other users' historical data only if it supplied its own historical data to the auditor or has never used the tool. The rule's three-year-use example permits either an own-data audit or a pooled audit with the user's contribution, but not test data where statistically significant historical data is available.
qs: A bias audit conducted pursuant to section 5-301 of this Chapter must use historical data of the AEDT.
The historical data used to conduct a bias audit may be from one or more employers or employment agencies that use the AEDT.
The employer may not rely on a bias audit conducted using test data.

kp.k: Test data is conditional and requires provenance disclosure
kp.d: Test data, defined as non-historical audit data, is permitted when historical data is insufficient for a statistically significant audit. Published summaries must explain why historical data was not used and how test data was generated and obtained. The examples clarify that audit renewal runs from the audit date, not the user's adoption date: an agency using a tool for 6 months and relying on a 10-month-old audit needs an update when that audit reaches 12 months.
qs: “Test data” means data used to conduct a bias audit that is not historical data.
If a bias audit uses test data, the summary of results of the bias audit must explain why historical data was not used and describe how the test data used was generated and obtained.

kp.k: Audit publication includes data, category results, and adoption date
kp.d: Before use, city employers and employment agencies must conspicuously publish the latest audit date and a results summary on their website's employment section, including data sources and explanations, unknown-category counts, category applicant or candidate counts, selection or scoring rates, and impact ratios. They must also publish the distribution date, meaning when they began using the specific AEDT. A clearly identified active hyperlink is permitted, and publication must continue for at least 6 months after the latest employment-decision use.
qs: “Distribution date” means the date the employer or employment agency began using a specific AEDT.

The requirements of subdivision (a) of this section may be met with an active hyperlink to a website containing the required summary of results and distribution date, provided that the link is clearly identified as a link to results of the bias audit.
An employer or employment agency must keep the summary of results and distribution date posted for at least 6 months after its latest use of the AEDT for an employment decision.

kp.k: Advance notice does not guarantee an alternative selection process
kp.d: For candidates and employees considered for promotion who reside in the city, the specified notice channels require at least 10 business days before AEDT use. Candidate channels include the employment website, job postings, or mail/email; employee channels include a provided written policy or procedure, job postings, or mail/email. Notices must explain how to request an alternative process or reasonable accommodation under other laws, if available, but these rules do not require an alternative process.
qs: Provide notice in a job posting at least 10 business days before use of an AEDT;
Nothing in this subchapter requires an employer or employment agency to provide an alternative selection process.

kp.k: Data transparency covers retention, collection, sources, and requests
kp.d: Employers and agencies must conspicuously provide information about AEDT data retention policies, collected data types, and data sources on their employment website. They must post instructions for written requests and supply information within 30 days of receiving a request. The rules also require explanations when disclosure would violate law or interfere with a law-enforcement investigation.
qs: Post instructions on the employment section of its website in a clear and conspicuous manner for how to make a written request for such information, and if a written request is received, provide such information within 30 days; and

Provide an explanation to a candidate for employment or employee being considered for promotion why disclosure of such information would violate local, state, or federal law, or interfere with a law enforcement investigation.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: DCWP establishes conditions for using automated tools in hiring and promotion, rather than predicting changes to legal services.
pts.d: This cross-domain source concerns employment decisions. DCWP states that Local Law 144 makes use of covered automated employment decision tools conditional on a recent bias audit, public audit information and notices. Covered decision-making includes sole reliance on a simplified output, weighting it more heavily than any other criterion, or using it to override other conclusions, including human judgments. The rule expressly reaches early-stage screening, not just final hiring decisions. These are regulatory requirements, not empirical claims that AI improves hiring or predictions that it replaces workers.

pts.k: DCWP requires demographic comparisons and public disclosure of audit results for covered employment tools.
pts.d: Selection or classification tools require category-specific selection rates and impact ratios; scoring tools require the full-sample median, category-specific rates of scoring above that median, and impact ratios. Comparisons must separately address sex, race/ethnicity and intersectional categories. Unknown-category counts must be reported. Before use, employers and employment agencies in the city must publish the latest audit date, a results summary and the tool's distribution date. The text specifies measurement and transparency obligations; it does not present evidence that these obligations eliminate bias or establish a minimum passing impact ratio.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source rests on legislative and administrative authority, not observed AI performance or labour-market evidence.
pts.d: DCWP invokes the NYC Charter and Administrative Code to implement Local Law 144 of 2021. It links the audit calculations to EEOC Uniform Guidelines and describes two rounds of proposals, hearings and public comments as the basis for revisions. Numerical tables illustrate how audits work; they are presented as examples, not findings from identified employers or measured deployments. There are no benchmarks, causal studies or forecasts of employment or legal-market effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2023 rule sets recurring audit and disclosure deadlines and qualifies which data and tools fall within its requirements.
pts.d: An audit cannot be more than one year old during use. Required notices for city-resident candidates and employees being considered for promotion must precede use by at least 10 business days; published audit information must remain available for at least six months after the latest use. Historical data are the default audit basis. An existing user relying on other employers' historical data must contribute its own historical data; a first-time user may rely on others' data without that contribution. Test data are permitted when historical data are insufficient for a statistically significant audit, with explanations of why and how test data were obtained. Auditors may omit categories representing less than 2% of audit data from impact-ratio calculations but must justify and disclose the omission and category counts and rates. Translation and transcription outputs are excluded from the definition of simplified output. No future forecast horizon or enforcement commencement date is stated in the supplied text.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Employers and employment agencies bear compliance duties; applicants and employees receive disclosures; auditors must satisfy independence requirements.
pts.d: The regulated users are employers and employment agencies using covered tools, including in screening and promotion. City-resident applicants for specific positions and employees considered for promotion receive advance notice and instructions for requesting alternatives or accommodations, but the rule itself does not require an alternative selection process. Auditors must exercise objective judgment and cannot have specified involvement, employment relationships or financial interests relating to the tool, its users or its vendor. The public gains access to audit summaries. Law firms are mentioned as commenters, not as evidence of changes to legal-service delivery or demand.
